source.title_on_document: GraphStory: Collaborative Story Writing through Event-Based Narrative Editing

paper_design_summary: A formative study recruited five writing-field students to revise a familiar story using a graph-and-LLM prototype and provide interview feedback (pp. 3-4, Sections 3.1-3.3). The main user study involved 16 writing-field students, each completing the same story-writing task with ChatGPT first and GraphStory second in a fixed, non-random order (p. 7, Sections 5.1-5.2). Evaluation used participant questionnaires and qualitative feedback on tool usability, useful-plot-point support, functionality, and perceived workload; no creativity or diversity measure was scored on the produced stories (pp. 7-9, Sections 5.2-5.4 and Figures 5-7).

studies.label: Formative study: interviews and graph-based story-editing prototype

assignment.what_was_assigned: Single-group procedure: participants completed an initial interview, used the same graph-based LLM prototype, and completed a follow-up interview; no comparison-condition allocation.
assignment.quote: Participants were first briefed on the study goals, then completed the initial interview, followed by a 30-minute interaction with the prototype with researcher support.
assignment.locator: p. 4, Section 3.2, Study Design and Procedure

arms.name: Graph-based LLM prototype
arms.description: Single formative-study condition. Five participants were recruited; a separate analyzed denominator is not stated (pp. 3-4, Sections 3.1-3.3).

participants.who: Five students in writing-related fields, including screenwriting, literature, and copywriting, were recruited. All had writing experience and prior LLM use. The text describes thematic analysis but does not separately state an analyzed participant count.
participants.quote: We recruited five participants (aged 18–22; 2 male, 3 female), all of whom were students majoring in writing-related fields, including screenwriting, literature, and copywriting.
participants.locator: p. 3, Section 3.1, Participants; p. 4, Section 3.3, Analysis

ai_tool.name_model: Graph-based prototype connected to an LLM; model not stated
ai_tool.how_used: Participants edited and reorganized a familiar story as a graph and could submit edits to an LLM to generate updated versions (p. 4, Section 3.2).

task.description: Modify and reorganize a familiar story with the graph-based prototype while thinking aloud; interviews examined writing practices and perceived usability/usefulness (pp. 3-4, Section 3.2).
task.duration: 30-minute prototype interaction, plus initial and follow-up interviews (p. 4, Section 3.2).

studies.label: Main user study: ChatGPT followed by GraphStory

assignment.what_was_assigned: Every participant used ChatGPT first and then GraphStory for the same task; the within-person tool order was fixed.
assignment.quote: Participants first wrote a story using ChatGPT and then completed the same task using our system.
assignment.locator: p. 7, Section 5.2, Study Design and Procedure

arms.name: ChatGPT
arms.description: First condition: story writing from supplied ideas using ChatGPT. The same participants subsequently used GraphStory (p. 7, Section 5.2; p. 8, Figure 5).

arms.name: GraphStory
arms.description: Second condition: the same story-writing task using the event-graph system with LLM generation. These are the same participants as in the ChatGPT condition (p. 7, Section 5.2; p. 8, Figure 5).

participants.who: Students majoring in writing-related fields with advanced writing skills and familiarity with AI writing tools; none had participated in a prior study involving this system. Figure 5 shows 16 responses per condition, from the same people. The methods identify students, despite the abstract describing professional and semi-professional writers.
participants.quote: We recruited 16 students aged 18 to 22 (8 male, 8 female) to participate in the study.
participants.locator: p. 7, Sections 5.1-5.2; p. 8, Figure 5 (16 responses per condition); p. 9, Figure 7 (number of responses)

ai_tool.name_model: GraphStory (GPT-4o) versus ChatGPT (baseline model not stated)
ai_tool.how_used: GraphStory supports editable event graphs, branching narrative flows, review of AI-added events, and generation of complete narrative text using GPT-4o. The baseline uses ChatGPT to complete the same writing task (p. 6, Sections 4.3-4.4; p. 7, Section 5.2).

task.description: Individually write a story from a set of provided ideas, first with ChatGPT and then repeat the same task with GraphStory, using a think-out-loud protocol in a private room with researcher support (p. 7, Section 5.2).
task.duration: Approximately one hour per study session; separate per-condition task durations are not stated (p. 7, Section 5.2).

eligibility.reason: The main comparison explicitly used ChatGPT first and GraphStory second for everyone, so generative-AI condition order was not randomized (p. 7, Section 5.2). It analyzed 16 people with repeated observations in both conditions, not separate groups (p. 7, Sections 5.1-5.2; p. 8, Figure 5); the separate formative study recruited only five people and reported no distinct analyzed count (pp. 3-4, Sections 3.1-3.3). Neither study reaches the 50-person threshold. The quantitative outcomes are participants' self-reports about the tools and workload, with qualitative interview feedback; the paper reports no scored creativity or diversity outcome for participants' stories (pp. 7-9, Sections 5.2-5.4, Figures 5-7). Context class is none because studies with only self-reported outcomes are omitted under codebook Section 3, even though the main comparison has a non-random within-person design.

one_line_finding: In the fixed-order study of 16 students, GraphStory received higher self-reported ratings for efficiency in providing useful plot points than ChatGPT (M = 6.25, SD = 1.03 versus M = 5.62, SD = 1.05; p < 0.05), with no output-scored creativity measure (p. 7, Sections 5.1-5.3.1; p. 8, Figure 5, Q3).
